overview: The single most important distinction in microbial control — because one guarantees zero survivors, and the other does not.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: The complete destruction or removal of all forms of microbial life, including bacterial endospores.
aspects.valueB: The reduction of pathogenic microorganisms to a level considered safe, typically on inanimate surfaces — spores usually survive.

aspects.label: Spore Elimination
aspects.valueA: Kills bacterial endospores, the most resistant microbial life form.
aspects.valueB: Does not reliably kill bacterial endospores.

aspects.label: Common Methods
aspects.valueA: Autoclaving (moist heat), dry heat ovens, gamma irradiation, ethylene oxide gas.
aspects.valueB: Chemical disinfectants (bleach, alcohols, phenolics), UV light, pasteurization.

aspects.label: Typical Application
aspects.valueA: Surgical instruments, culture media, anything entering sterile body sites or requiring a sterile culture.
aspects.valueB: Countertops, non-critical medical equipment, floors — surfaces that don't need to be sterile, just safe.

aspects.label: Verification
aspects.valueA: Confirmed with biological indicators (e.g. Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore strips) or chemical indicators.
aspects.valueB: Verified indirectly, by adherence to contact time and concentration, not by spore-kill testing.

aspects.label: Absolute vs Relative Standard
aspects.valueA: An absolute, all-or-nothing standard — an item is either sterile or it is not.
aspects.valueB: A relative standard — 'clean enough' varies by disinfectant level (low, intermediate, high) and intended use.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Eliminates all life forms, including spores.
aspects.valueB: Reduces pathogen load but does not guarantee spore kill.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: If spores survive, it's disinfection, not sterilization — no exceptions.
